title: Latency Optimization & Batching
summary: An agent's latency is dominated by output tokens (generation is sequential), the number of loop iterations, and tool round-trips. You attack each: shrink and structure the output, parallelize independent tool calls, cache repeated work, and route simple steps to smaller/faster models. For work that isn't user-facing, you batch requests together to trade per-request latency for throughput and lower cost.

subtopics.title: Latency has three big sources: tokens, loops, tools
subtopics.explanation: An agent's wall-clock time is roughly the sum of generation time (proportional to output tokens), the latency of each tool call, and the number of times it goes around the loop. Profiling which of the three dominates for your agent tells you where to spend effort. You can't optimize latency meaningfully until you know whether you're token-bound, loop-bound, or tool-bound.
subtopics.example:
import time

def timed_agent(goal):
    t0 = time.time()
    steps = 0
    while not done(goal):
        t_gen = time.time()
        step = model.generate(goal)      # token-bound time
        gen_ms = (time.time() - t_gen) * 1000
        t_tool = time.time()
        run_tool(step)                   # tool round-trip time
        tool_ms = (time.time() - t_tool) * 1000
        print(f"step {steps}: gen={gen_ms:.0f}ms tool={tool_ms:.0f}ms")
        steps += 1
    print(f"total={(time.time()-t0)*1000:.0f}ms over {steps} steps")

subtopics.title: Output tokens dominate — generation is sequential
subtopics.explanation: Input tokens are processed in parallel, but output tokens are produced one at a time, so a 500-token answer costs far more latency than a 5000-token prompt. The biggest single lever is usually making the model say less: terser system prompts, structured (not prose) outputs, and asking only for what you need. Cutting output length is the highest-leverage latency fix precisely because generation can't be parallelized.
subtopics.example:
# slow: verbose free-form answer, hundreds of output tokens
prompt_v1 = "Explain in detail why you chose this action and then act."

# fast: compact structured output, a handful of tokens
prompt_v2 = "Respond ONLY as JSON: {\"action\": <name>, \"args\": {...}}"
# fewer output tokens -> lower generation latency,
# and the JSON is also easier for code to consume

subtopics.title: Parallelize independent tool calls and steps
subtopics.explanation: When an agent needs several tool results that don't depend on each other, running them sequentially wastes time equal to the sum of their latencies; running them concurrently costs only the slowest one. Modern models can even emit multiple tool calls in a single turn so you can dispatch them together. Parallelizing independent work turns a chain of round-trips into one round-trip's worth of waiting.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio

async def gather_context(order_id, user_id):
    # these three lookups don't depend on each other
    order, profile, inventory = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch_order(order_id),
        fetch_profile(user_id),
        fetch_inventory(),
    )
    # total latency ~= the slowest call, not the sum of all three
    return order, profile, inventory

subtopics.title: Cache repeated work and use smaller, faster models
subtopics.explanation: Much of an agent's traffic is repetitive — the same system prompt, the same lookups, near-identical questions — so caching responses and reusing a stable prompt prefix eliminates whole model calls. In parallel, routing easy steps (classification, extraction, formatting) to a smaller, faster model cuts per-token time sharply. Combining caching with right-sized models attacks both the number of calls and the cost of each call.
subtopics.example:
cache = {}

def cached_classify(text):
    if text in cache:                 # skip the model entirely
        return cache[text]
    # a small fast model is plenty for classification
    label = small_model.classify(text)
    cache[text] = label
    return label
# heavy reasoning still goes to the big model elsewhere

subtopics.title: Batch offline work for throughput over latency
subtopics.explanation: When results aren't needed immediately — nightly enrichment, bulk extraction, evaluation runs — you submit many requests together through a batch API instead of one at a time. You accept higher per-request latency (minutes to hours) in exchange for much higher throughput and typically lower cost per token. Batching is the right tool whenever throughput and cost matter more than a fast individual response.
subtopics.example:
# online: one request, needs to be fast (user waiting)
result = model.generate(user_prompt)

# offline: thousands of requests, latency doesn't matter
job = model.batch_submit([
    {"id": row.id, "prompt": build_prompt(row)}
    for row in dataset            # e.g. 50k rows overnight
])
results = model.batch_wait(job)   # cheaper per token, high throughput

foundations.overview: Agent latency is not one number but the sum of three components you can measure and attack separately: token-generation time, loop iterations, and tool round-trips. Generation time is the usual bottleneck because output tokens are produced sequentially — the model emits one token, conditions on it, then emits the next — so a long answer is expensive in a way a long prompt (processed in parallel) is not. That makes cutting output the single highest-leverage fix: terse prompts, structured rather than prose responses, and asking only for the fields you need. The next lever is concurrency: tool calls and sub-tasks that don't depend on one another should run in parallel so the agent waits for the slowest, not the sum. Then comes reuse — caching responses and reusing a stable prompt prefix removes whole calls — and right-sizing, where easy steps like classification or extraction go to a smaller, faster model while only hard reasoning uses the frontier model. Finally, for work that no user is waiting on, batching flips the trade-off: you submit many requests together through a batch API, accepting minutes-to-hours latency in exchange for higher throughput and lower cost per token. The discipline is to profile first, identify whether you are token-, loop-, or tool-bound, and apply the matching technique rather than optimizing blindly.
foundations.formalDefinition: Agent latency is the wall-clock time from request to final answer, decomposable as the sum over loop steps of generation time (proportional to output tokens) plus tool round-trip time; batching is the technique of submitting many independent requests together to maximize throughput and reduce per-token cost at the expense of per-request latency.
foundations.whyItMatters: Latency determines whether an agent is usable in an interactive setting and how much it costs to run at scale; because output-token generation is sequential and loops multiply it, uncontrolled latency compounds quickly, and batching is what makes large offline agent workloads economically feasible.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the agent as a worker who must write every answer by hand (output tokens, one stroke at a time) but can read instantly (input tokens, in parallel). To go faster you make them write less, let several assistants fetch facts at once (parallel tools), keep a drawer of answers they've written before (cache), hand routine notes to a junior (small model), and for a giant stack of forms, mail them all off overnight rather than filling each while someone waits (batching).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Interactive assistants trimming output and parallelizing lookups to feel responsive, pipelines routing classification to small models, RAG systems caching embeddings and stable prompt prefixes, and data teams running nightly batch jobs to enrich or label millions of records cheaply.
commonUseCases: Cutting output tokens and using structured outputs to reduce generation time
Parallelizing independent tool calls within a single agent turn
Routing easy steps to smaller/faster models to cut per-token latency
Batching non-interactive bulk work for throughput and lower cost

commonMisconceptions.myth: A shorter prompt is the main way to cut latency.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Input tokens are processed in parallel and are cheap in time; output tokens are generated sequentially and dominate latency. Cutting the response length usually matters far more than shortening the prompt.

Batching optimizes throughput and cost, not per-request latency — individual requests often take minutes to hours. It's for offline work where no user is waiting, the opposite of interactive latency tuning.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should always use the biggest, best model.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Frontier models are slower and pricier per token. Easy steps (classification, extraction, formatting) run well on smaller, faster models; reserving the big model for hard reasoning cuts latency and cost.

checkpoints.prompt: Which change usually cuts an agent's latency the most?
options: Shortening the input prompt by half
Reducing the number of output tokens the model generates
checkpoints.explanation: Output tokens are generated sequentially (one conditioned on the last), so response length dominates latency. Input tokens are processed in parallel and are comparatively cheap in time, so trimming the output beats trimming the prompt.

checkpoints.prompt: When is a batch API the right choice?
options: For a live chat response the user is waiting on
For nightly enrichment of a million records where per-request speed doesn't matter
To reduce time-to-first-token in a UI
To parallelize two dependent tool calls
checkpoints.explanation: Batching trades per-request latency (minutes to hours) for high throughput and lower cost per token, which fits offline bulk work. It is the wrong tool for anything interactive where a user is waiting.

checkpoints.prompt: Three independent tool lookups take 200ms, 350ms, and 500ms. Roughly how long if run concurrently vs sequentially?
checkpoints.explanation: Sequential latency is the sum (200+350+500 = 1050ms). Run concurrently with asyncio.gather, the total is about the slowest call (500ms), since the independent lookups overlap.

keyTakeaways: Agent latency = generation time (output tokens) + tool round-trips + loop iterations; profile to find which dominates.
Output tokens are generated sequentially, so cutting response length (terse prompts, structured outputs) is the highest-leverage fix.
Run independent tool calls and sub-tasks concurrently so you wait for the slowest, not the sum.
Cache repeated work and route easy steps to smaller/faster models, reserving the frontier model for hard reasoning.
For offline bulk work, batch requests to maximize throughput and cut per-token cost — never batch interactive requests.
